offence_severity: Life imprisonment and fine of Rs.5000/- each, in default of payment, further to undergo rigorous imprisonment for one year
physical_harm: The deceased's body was found mutilated with the right hand and head missing
number_of_offences: Three offences charged under Sections 302, 364 and 120-B IPC, all upheld
premeditation_planning: The court found premeditation/planning based on the motive of enmity and threats
motive: Enmity between the complainant and accused, and threat given by accused to finish the family of complainant
key_evidence_accepted: Cogent and acceptable evidence adduced by prosecution has established the deceased last seen with accused, recovery of incriminating articles pursuant to disclosure statements of accused, motive for the crime, i.e. enmity between complaint and accused and threat given by accused to finish the family of complainant
witness_credibility: The prosecution very much relied on PWs 3, 4 and 10 to prove the last seen theory and the courts below rightly accepted their version. This Court is satisfied that the prosecution has succeeded in establishing the circumstance of last seen theory
trial_duration: Dates of offence: 15.4.1998; Trial judgment: 31.01.2002; High Court decision: 02.03.2006; Supreme Court decision: 22.03.2013
legal_representation: Seeraj Bagga for the Appellant; Shovan Mishra and Milind Kumar for the Respondent
investigation_status: FIR registered, charge sheet filed, trial completed
appeal_history: Trial court: Conviction and sentence; High Court: Affirmed conviction and sentence; Supreme Court: Dismissed appeals
prosecution_argument: The prosecution case rests solely on circumstantial evidence, including the deceased being last seen with the accused, recovery of incriminating articles pursuant to the information given by the accused, and motive for the crime, i.e., enmity between the complainant and the accused and threats given by the accused to finish the family of the complainant.
defence_argument: The learned amicus curiae for the appellants contended that in the absence of direct evidence, the slightest discrepancy depicting the possibility of two views would exculpate the accused on the basis of the benefit of doubt.
legal_principle_applied: The Supreme Court applied the five golden principles laid down in Sharad Birdhichand Sarda v. State of Maharashtra, which require that the circumstances from which the conclusion of guilt is drawn must be fully established, consistent only with the hypothesis of the accused's guilt, of a conclusive nature, exclude every possible hypothesis except the one to be proved, and form a chain of evidence so complete as not to leave any reasonable ground for the conclusion consistent with the innocence of the accused.
precedent_relied_upon: Sharad Birdhichand Sarda v. State of Maharashtra, 1985 (1) SCR 88 = (1984) 4 SCC 116
sentencing_rationale: The trial court rightly accepted the prosecution case and awarded life sentence which was rightly affirmed by the High Court. The Supreme Court is satisfied that the prosecution has established all the circumstances by cogent and acceptable evidence and it leads to a conclusion that it were the appellants/accused who kidnapped and committed the murder of the deceased.
